title: Turk Shahis
capsule: The Turk Shahis (also called the Kabul Shahis) were a dynasty of Western Turkic origin that ruled the Kabul valley, Gandhara, and Zabulistan in the eastern Hindu Kush. They emerged around 665 CE when Barha Tegin seized power amid the collapse of Nezak Hun authority following Arab raids under Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura, and for over a century-and-a-half they blocked Arab-Muslim expansion north of the Hindu Kush from a court centered on Kapisa and Kabul, where a syncretic Shaivite-Buddhist culture flourished. The line ended around 822 CE when the last ruler, Lagaturman, was deposed by his Brahmin minister Kallar, who founded the Hindu Shahi dynasty; the southern Zunbil branch fell to the Saffarids of Sistan about 870. The dataset's 561 start-date predates the dynasty's actual mid-7th-century rise and reflects the earlier Western Turk/Hephthalite background rather than Turk Shahi rule itself.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Turk Shahis' core territory in the Kabul and Laghman valleys is attested by Chinese pilgrim accounts (Xuanzang, 630 CE), Arab geographical texts, and coin finds; the southern and eastern extents into Zabulistan and toward the Indus are reconstructed from narrative sources and carry significant uncertainty.
